46-007.r: ATP → ADP (ATP hydrolysis) gives the body maximum energy; ATP is the high-energy molecule that stores energy for muscle work and biosynthesis.

46-008.r: Respiration converts biochemical energy from nutrients into ATP (Adenosine Triphosphate) and releases waste products.

46-009.r: Aerobic respiration → complete breakdown of glucose with oxygen into CO2 and H2O, releasing a large amount of energy; goes on all the time in plant and animal cells.

46-010.r: Glycolysis in cytoplasm: glucose → pyruvate (three carbons, not four). No oxygen → lactic acid (in muscles) or CO2 + ethanol. True: (ii) and (iii).
46-010.t: Pyruvate has three carbon atoms; statement (i) wrongly says four.

46-011.r: Book's answer: lungs maintain body temperature – breathing exhales CO2 and vaporises body water, while food oxidation in tissues produces energy.

47-001.r: Normal heart rate ≈ 72-75 beats per minute; during sleep a slow rate of 40-50 BPM is common.

47-002.r: Heart rests between two beats: each beat = contraction (pumps blood out) + relaxation (draws blood in).

47-003.r: Heart attack (myocardial infarction) signs: chest pain, pain in arms, back, neck, jaw; shortness of breath, cold sweat, nausea. Leg pain is not a symptom.

47-005.r: Heart has four chambers: upper left and right atria + lower left and right ventricles (in humans, other mammals and birds); valves stop backflow.

47-006.r: Human heart = only four chambers: right and left atria (upper) receive blood; more muscular right and left ventricles (lower) pump it out.

47-007.r: Heartbeat starts in the heart itself: the sinus node in the right atrium sends electrical signals, acting as a natural pacemaker.

47-008.r: Wrist pulse beats at the same rate as the heart; pulse rate = number of heartbeats per minute (bpm).

47-009.r: First heart transplant → Dr. Christian Barnard (Bernard), South Africa; on Louis Washkansky, 3 December 1967, Groote Schuur Hospital, Cape Town.

47-012.r: Jarvik-7 → first successful permanent artificial heart, invented by Robert Jarvik; first implanted in Barney Clark in 1982.

47-013.r: Pacemaker → small device placed in chest or abdomen; its electrical pulses keep the heart beating at a normal rate (regulates heartbeat).

47-014.r: SA (sino-atrial) node = natural pacemaker of the heart; lies in the right atrium and starts each heartbeat.
47-014.t: Don't confuse the SA node (pacemaker) with the AV node or Bundle of His given in the options.

47-015.r: Pulmonary vein → only vein with oxygenated blood (lungs → left atrium); pulmonary artery → only artery with oxygen-poor blood.
47-015.h: Pulmonary vessels break the rule: vein carries pure blood, artery carries impure blood.

47-016.r: Total blood volume of a normal 70 kg adult → 5-6 litres.

47-018.r: Blood → fluid connective tissue: matrix is plasma, no fibres; carries oxygen from lungs to tissues and CO2 back to lungs.

47-020.r: Erythrocytes (RBCs) help blood circulation: their haemoglobin carries oxygen from lungs to all tissues and brings CO2 back to the lungs.

47-021.r: Plasma → straw-coloured fluid part of blood; blood ≈ 55% plasma + 45% cells; plasma is over 90% water.

47-022.r: Both true: blood = plasma (about 55%) + formed elements (45%: RBCs, WBCs, platelets); haemoglobin in RBCs makes blood red.

47-023.r: Haemoglobin → protein in red blood cells (found in human blood); carries oxygen from lungs to tissues and CO2 back to lungs.

47-024.r: Haemoglobin is slightly alkaline, not acidic (solution pH 7.1-7.4); red, iron-containing protein; 12-16 g per 100 ml of blood.

47-025.r: RBCs (erythrocytes): contain iron (haemoglobin), give blood its red colour, carry oxygen; they do not give immunity. Haemoglobin's job → transport of oxygen.

47-028.r: Myoglobin → oxygen-binding heme protein of skeletal muscle; contains iron (Fe); higher oxygen affinity than haemoglobin.

47-030.r: Earthworm (phylum Annelida) → haemoglobin dissolved in plasma; it has a closed circulatory system.

47-031.r: Blood (and RBCs) are red due to haemoglobin combined with oxygen; RBCs (erythrocytes) have no nucleus and occur only in vertebrates.

47-033.r: Blood's key function → takes oxygen (bound to haemoglobin in red cells) to all parts; also carries nutrients like glucose, amino acids, fatty acids.

47-034.r: Normal average blood pressure → 120/80 mm Hg (systolic 120, diastolic 80).

47-036.r: Sphygmomanometer → measures blood pressure (inflatable cuff + mercury or mechanical manometer, used with a stethoscope).
47-036.t: Don't confuse sphygmomanometer with the look-alike options spherometer and anemometer.

47-038.r: In 'BP 140 mm Hg', Hg = mercury; blood pressure is measured in millimetres of mercury (mmHg); normal 120/80 mmHg.

47-039.r: Blood pressure generally increases with age; other factors: smoking, obesity, too much salt or alcohol, stress, family history, kidney disease.

47-040.r: Normal BP 120/80 → Mr. Y; Mrs. X (90/60) is below normal; Mr. X (160/120) and Mrs. Y (140/100) are above normal.

47-041.r: Blood pressure is greater than atmospheric pressure: the 120 mm Hg reading is the excess over atmospheric pressure (760 mm Hg).

47-042.r: Blood groups discovered by Karl Landsteiner (Austrian) in 1900; with Alexander Wiener he found the Rh factor (1937), named after the rhesus monkey.

47-044.r: Blood group is set by antigens on the RBC surface (ABO and Rh systems), not haemoglobin, RBC shape or WBC-RBC mix → 'None of the above'.

47-045.r: Blood group O RBCs carry neither agglutinogen (antigen) A nor B; group A carries A, group B carries B.

47-046.r: Universal donor → blood group O: its RBCs have neither A nor B antigens, so it can be given to any group.

47-049.r: AB = universal recipient: RBCs have both A and B antigens (so the Reason is false) but plasma has no antibodies; accepts blood from any group.

47-053.r: Group A can receive only from A or O → wife (O), son (A) and daughter (O) can donate; brother (AB) cannot.

47-054.r: Emergency transfusion, group unknown → give O negative (O, Rh–): group O RBCs have no A or B antigens.

47-056.r: Couple AB+ and O– → their twins are A+ and B+; so the adopted son is the O+ one.

47-057.r: Father A × mother O → child O or A (book's answer: O); Bernstein (1924) showed ABO groups follow Mendel's laws.

47-058.r: Transfusion blood must match in ABO type and Rh factor; Rh antigen (like rhesus monkey's) is on RBCs of nearly 80% of humans (Rh+ve).

47-059.r: Rh incompatibility (erythroblastosis fetalis) → Rh-negative mother carrying an Rh-positive foetus; baby may get severe anaemia.

47-063.r: Antigen → foreign substance (usually protein, sometimes polysaccharide) that triggers the immune system and stimulates formation of specific antibodies.

47-066.r: WBCs (white blood corpuscles) protect from infection and build disease resistance: they reach the infected site and destroy bacteria and viruses.

47-068.r: Lymphocytes → form antibodies in plasma; most important immunity cells; about 20-25% of WBCs; include T cells, B cells, natural killer cells.

47-071.r: IgM → first antibody produced in a new (primary) infection; five classes of immunoglobulins: IgG, IgM, IgA, IgE, IgD.

47-072.r: B cells and T cells (lymphocytes of adaptive immunity) → protect the body from diseases caused by pathogens.

47-073.r: Vaccination → antibodies are made only by B cells (B lymphocytes); T cells destroy pathogens and coordinate the immune response.

47-074.r: Viscosity of blood → mainly due to proteins in plasma (and hematocrit); plasma viscosity depends on water and protein content.

47-075.r: WBC diameter ≈ 0.007 mm; normal WBC count 4,000-11,000 per microlitre (about 1% of blood volume); excess = leukocytosis, shortage = leukopenia.

47-076.r: Leukemia → cancer starting in bone marrow; very high numbers of abnormal, immature WBCs (blasts).
47-076.t: Don't confuse leukemia (excess abnormal WBCs) with anaemia, anoxia or septicemia.

47-077.r: RBCs are formed in red bone marrow (erythropoiesis, about 2 million per second); in the embryo the liver is the main site.

47-078.r: Spleen → forms WBCs (lymphocytes) and destroys old RBCs (RBC life 100-120 days); acts as a blood filter. Lymphocytes also form elsewhere ('more than one').

47-081.r: Coronary arteries → supply oxygen-rich blood to heart muscle (myocardium); cardiac veins remove its deoxygenated blood.

47-082.r: Thrombin → enzyme of blood clotting; converts fibrinogen → fibrin; formed from prothrombin (coagulation factor II).

47-084.r: Plasma ≈ 91-92% water (answer 90%); plasma ≈ 55% of blood volume; contains albumin, fibrinogen, globulins.

47-085.r: Blood has more platelets (150,000-350,000 per microlitre) than WBCs; platelets help clotting and are only about 20% of RBC diameter.

47-086.r: Nitric oxide (NO) → made in the body from L-arginine by NO synthase, mainly in blood-vessel lining (endothelium); dilates vessels, increases blood flow.
47-086.t: Don't confuse nitric oxide (NO) with nitrous oxide or nitrogen dioxide in the options.

47-087.r: Alum stops bleeding from cuts: blood is a colloid and alum's aluminium ions have high coagulating power → A and R true, R explains A.

47-088.r: Artificial 'plastic blood' usable for any blood group → University of Sheffield, Britain; light, needs no cooling, keeps longer.

48-001.r: Liver → detoxifies alcohol and other harmful substances through complex chemical reactions.

48-002.r: Healthy adult excretes about 1.5 litres of urine per day (24 hours); urine is 91-96% water.

48-003.r: Yellow colour of urine → pigment urochrome (also called urobilin).

48-004.r: Only 2 true: filtrate from Bowman's capsule passes tubules that reabsorb glucose; cleaner blood leaves by the renal vein, not renal artery.
48-004.t: Renal artery brings waste-laden blood to the kidney; renal vein takes cleaned blood away.

48-005.r: Dialysis → artificial blood purification (removes waste and excess water) that replaces lost kidney function in kidney failure.

48-007.r: Dialyzer = artificial kidney: moves solutes and water across a semipermeable membrane between blood and dialysate. Kidney failure options: peritoneal dialysis, hemodialysis, transplant.

48-008.r: All the body's blood is filtered through the kidneys: they remove water-soluble wastes (urea, ammonium) and reabsorb water, glucose, amino acids.

48-009.r: Urea is separated from blood in the kidney (ultrafiltration in the renal capsule), forming dilute urine.

48-010.r: Kidneys → main organs of the excretory system; they filter blood and remove waste products.

48-011.r: About 1200 ml (cc) of blood flows through both kidneys per minute, forming about 1 ml urine; daily ≈ 1500 litres blood purified, 1.5 litres urine.

48-012.r: Kidney failure → nitrogenous wastes (ammonia, urea, uric acid) accumulate in the blood.

48-013.r: Blood sugar regulation is the pancreas's job (insulin), not the kidney's; kidneys regulate blood water, filter urea and secrete hormones.

48-014.r: Main compound of human kidney stones → calcium oxalate (forms envelope-shaped crystals; called raphides in plants).

48-015.r: Kidney stones form by crystallisation of oxalates; most common = calcium oxalate. Four types: calcium oxalate, uric acid, struvite, cystine.

48-018.r: Sweat excretes many elements – sodium, potassium, calcium, magnesium and traces of zinc, copper, iron – so the answer is 'more than one'.

48-019.r: Kidney transplant immunosuppressant (anti-rejection) → monoclonal antibodies (mAbs), used as induction therapy.

49-001.r: Humans have 12 pairs of cranial nerves; they exit the cranium from the ventral (bottom) surface of the brain.

49-002.r: Spinal nerves → 31 pairs (mixed nerves: motor, sensory, autonomic); grouped as cervical, thoracic, lumbar, sacral, coccygeal.

49-003.r: Input and output nerves meet in the central nervous system, especially the spinal cord, where reflex arcs form.

49-004.r: Brain does all three: cerebrum → thinking, speech, learning; cerebellum → balance and posture; brainstem → automatic functions like heartbeat.

49-006.r: Reflex action is governed by the spinal cord: sensory neurons synapse there, so reflexes skip the brain and act quickly.

49-007.r: Brain feels no pain when pricked by a needle – it has no pain or touch receptors of its own.

49-008.r: Memory, thinking, feeling, movement → cerebrum (largest part of brain); cerebellum (smaller, at back) → coordination.

49-009.r: Cerebellum = 'little brain'; lies below cerebral hemispheres, behind pons-medulla; controls balance, coordination, muscle tone, motor learning.

49-010.r: Satiety and thirst centres → hypothalamus; it also governs body temperature, hunger, sleep, circadian rhythm, moods and hormone release.

49-011.r: Hypothalamus regulates body temperature (normal 98.6°F); also hunger, thirst, fatigue, sleep, circadian rhythms.
49-011.t: Don't confuse hypothalamus with thalamus (option a).

49-012.r: Body temperature stays constant (98.6°F / 37°C) in winter and summer; the hypothalamus acts as the body's thermostat.

49-013.r: Normal body temperature = 98.6°F = 37°C = 310 K; options 98.4, 98, 98.8°F are wrong → 'None of the above'.

49-015.r: Medulla oblongata (about three cm) → reflex centre for swallowing, vomiting, coughing, sneezing; links brain to spinal cord.

50-001.r: Endocrine glands = ductless glands; secrete hormones directly into blood (pineal, pituitary, thymus, thyroid, parathyroid, adrenal).

50-002.r: Hormones (chemical messengers) → secreted by endocrine glands; control growth, metabolism, reproduction, water balance, blood pressure.

50-003.r: Pituitary → smallest endocrine gland among options: about 0.5 g, 10 mm (pea-sized), in sella turcica at base of brain; called 'Master gland'.

50-005.r: Pancreas = mixed gland: endocrine (insulin, glucagon, somatostatin) + exocrine (pancreatic juice into duodenum via pancreatic duct).

50-006.r: Corpus luteum → temporary endocrine structure in the ovary; forms from follicle after ovulation; makes progesterone (high), estradiol, inhibin A.

50-007.r: Androgens (mainly testosterone) → secreted by Leydig (interstitial) cells next to the seminiferous tubules of the testis.
50-007.t: Don't confuse Leydig cells (androgen) with Sertoli cells (option a).

50-008.r: Gonads → progesterone; pituitary → growth hormone; pancreas → insulin; adrenal → cortisol.

50-009.r: ADH (antidiuretic hormone) from the pituitary controls the amount of urine from the kidney.

50-010.r: Progesterone → ovaries; testosterone → testes; thyroxine → thyroid; insulin → pancreas.

50-011.r: Blood sugar stays constant despite a carbohydrate-rich diet → insulin from pancreas beta cells; lack of insulin → diabetes, excess → hypoglycemia.

50-012.r: Defective pancreas → insulin (beta cells) and glucagon (alpha cells) not formed; delta cells of islets of Langerhans make somatostatin.

50-013.r: Secretin (peptide hormone from S cells of duodenum) → stimulates pancreas to make digestive juice; also inhibits gastric acid.

50-014.r: Insulin = protein (peptide hormone) of 51 amino acids from beta cells of islets of Langerhans; main anabolic hormone.

50-015.r: Beta cells of islets of Langerhans (pancreas) → insulin; it moves glucose from blood into liver, fat and muscle cells.

50-016.r: Insulin controls metabolism of carbohydrates, fats and proteins → 'more than one' (BPSC key said only carbohydrates); insulin = peptide protein from islets of Langerhans.

50-023.r: Metal ion present in insulin → zinc.

50-024.r: Dahlia roots store inulin (a carbohydrate), not insulin; insulin comes from beta (β) cells of the pancreas. Exam answer: roots of dahlia (an inulin-insulin mix-up).
50-024.c: Dahlia roots store inulin, a carbohydrate, not the hormone insulin; the exam's answer (b) rests on this inulin-insulin mix-up.

50-025.r: Wrong pair: gastrin – blood pressure; gastrin stimulates gastric acid. Correct: insulin – blood glucose; melatonin – sleep; oxytocin – milk release.

50-026.r: Mother hugging or nursing her baby → oxytocin ('love' or 'cuddle' hormone); it also causes uterine contractions in childbirth.

50-027.r: Oxytocin → release of milk from mammary glands; targets uterus and breast; stretches cervix and uterus during labour.

50-028.r: Oxytocin is misused to raise milk yield in cattle, to enlarge vegetables and fruits (pumpkins, watermelons) and to speed up labour.

50-029.r: Oxytocin is a peptide hormone (neuropeptide), not a protein; keratin (hair, nails), fibroin (silk) and collagen are proteins.

50-030.r: Oxytocin (brand Pitocin) is injected into cows and buffaloes to make milk descend to the udders.

50-031.r: Oxytocin → made in hypothalamus (supraoptic and paraventricular nuclei), released by the posterior pituitary gland.
